name: IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL
meaning: A driver tried to read or write memory at an address it was not allowed to use, or at an invalid kernel priority level. The message names the driver responsible and the memory location involved. This is one of the most frequently seen stop codes on real machines and almost always points to RAM or a driver rather than Windows itself.
causes: Faulty RAM, or memory running at unstable XMP/EXPO timings
Corrupt or mismatched graphics, network, storage or antivirus driver
Overclocked CPU or undervolted GPU producing unstable results
A driver that does not match its hardware, such as an old Wi-Fi card driver
fix_steps: Write down the address and driver filename shown at the bottom of the blue screen, then search this site for that filename
Test RAM with MemTest86 for at least two full passes, with XMP/EXPO disabled while testing
Clean reinstall GPU drivers using DDU in Safe Mode
Update drivers in this order: chipset, graphics, network, then peripherals
Uninstall third-party antivirus, VPN clients and system tuning tools one at a time and retest
Run chkdsk C: /scan from an elevated prompt and check the drive's SMART data
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth followed by sfc /scannow
when_to_call_pro: Bring it to a technician if the named driver is a Microsoft system file and both memory and disk tests come back clean, because that usually means failing hardware.

name: DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL
meaning: The same class of fault as IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL, but reached through a different code path. A kernel-mode driver accessed memory it was not allowed to, usually after being handed a corrupt pointer. The named driver is almost always the culprit.
causes: Buggy or mismatched network, graphics or storage driver
Faulty RAM feeding the driver bad data
Antivirus or security software hooking the kernel and conflicting
Old driver package left behind by a previous device
fix_steps: Note the driver file named on the blue screen, for example tcpip.sys, ntoskrnl.exe or nvlddmkm.sys
Boot into Safe Mode and update or cleanly reinstall the matching driver; for graphics use DDU
Update chipset and network drivers, since most unexpected stop codes trace back to these
Uninstall third-party antivirus, VPN and tuning software one at a time and retest
Test RAM with MemTest86 and check disk health with chkdsk
Run sfc /scannow and DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the fault survives a clean driver install and a full memory test with all overclocks removed.

name: MEMORY_MANAGEMENT
meaning: Windows found corruption in the structures it uses to track memory itself, the page tables. Almost always defective RAM, but it can also follow a bad driver or a failing drive returning corrupt files.
causes: Defective RAM module, or a slot with dirty or bent contacts
Unstable memory timings under XMP or EXPO, or mismatched module speeds
Corrupt graphics driver or a hardware-accelerated application fault
Failing SSD returning corrupted system files
Incorrect page file settings or a nearly full system drive
fix_steps: Run mdsched.exe and let Windows Memory Diagnostic complete a full pass, then confirm with MemTest86
Reseat every RAM stick, clean the slots with a soft brush or compressed air, then try one stick at a time in each slot
Disable XMP/EXPO and run at the JEDEC default speed to rule out timings
Clean reinstall GPU drivers with DDU and update chipset drivers
Check free space on the system drive and set the page file to system-managed
Run sfc /scannow and DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth from an elevated prompt
when_to_call_pro: Escalate if MemTest86 reports even a single error, if the fault follows one stick across multiple slots, or if there is no overclock profile to disable.

name: PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA
meaning: Windows tried to use memory that should never be touched by ordinary code. One of the most common stop codes, and almost always a bad RAM module or a faulty driver. The bottom of the blue screen names the file and module responsible.
causes: Defective RAM, or RAM running at unstable timings
Corrupt or mismatched drivers, especially graphics and network
Failing SSD or HDD returning bad data
Insufficient or misconfigured page file on a memory-hungry system
fix_steps: Read the message at the bottom of the screen; it names the file such as win32k.sys or nvlddmkm.sys
Run Windows Memory Diagnostic, then confirm with MemTest86 over at least two passes
Disable XMP/EXPO and any overclock, then retest
Clean reinstall GPU drivers with DDU, plus a chipset driver update
Verify the system drive has free space and run chkdsk C: /scan
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth followed by sfc /scannow
when_to_call_pro: Take it in if memory tests are clean but crashes persist after a clean driver install, or if several different stop codes appear at once.

name: SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION
meaning: Windows tried to switch from kernel mode back to normal mode and hit an unexpected error. Frequently caused by graphics driver faults and faulty RAM. The bracketed value narrows down the exact area.
causes: Graphics driver corruption or a partially failed update
Corrupt system file in the graphics or networking stack
Overheating causing the GPU to drop out mid-operation
Incompatible third-party overlay or antivirus software
fix_steps: Identify the bracketed code, since 0xE, 0x50 and 0x1E are the most common, and search this site for it
Reinstall the graphics driver with DDU in Safe Mode
Update chipset drivers, then run sfc /scannow and DISM RestoreHealth
Test your RAM and check GPU temperatures under load
Remove overlays, screen recorders and background optimisation tools
Install any pending Windows updates, which sometimes fix known driver faults
when_to_call_pro: Seek help if the stop code appears during games or video calls and persists with a clean driver, since that points to the GPU or its power supply.

name: KMODE_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED
meaning: An error occurred in kernel mode that Windows had no handler for. The most common single meaning is a bad graphics driver, and the bracketed code narrows it further.
causes: Graphics driver fault, often right after a driver update
Corrupt system files or a failing drive
fix_steps: Clean reinstall the GPU driver using DDU in Safe Mode
Update chipset drivers before anything else
Test RAM with MemTest86 and check disk health
Reset all overclock and undervolt settings, including BIOS settings
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow
when_to_call_pro: Take it to a technician if the crash only happens under graphics load and survives a clean driver install at stock clocks.

name: SYSTEM_THREAD_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED
meaning: A system thread hit an error the kernel had no handler for. The hexadecimal value in brackets names the exact fault. In practice it nearly always points to a faulty driver or bad RAM rather than a broken Windows install.
causes: Faulty RAM or unstable XMP/EXPO memory timings
Corrupt or mismatched graphics, Wi-Fi or antivirus drivers
Bad system file after a partial Windows Update
Overclocked CPU or undervolted GPU producing unstable results
fix_steps: Write down the hex code in brackets, then search this site for it, since it identifies the exact driver or memory area at fault
Boot into Safe Mode using three interrupted boots or Shift+Restart, then run sfc /scannow and DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
Test RAM with Windows Memory Diagnostic or MemTest86 for at least two full passes
Remove any XMP/EXPO profile and all CPU/GPU overclocks, then retest
Reinstall your GPU driver cleanly using DDU in Safe Mode
Uninstall recently added drivers and software, especially audio, network and antivirus filter drivers
when_to_call_pro: Get help if the crash survives a clean driver install and a memory test with all overclocks removed, or if it points at a specific hardware part.

name: CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED
meaning: A process Windows cannot run without has stopped. Common after interrupted updates, failed antivirus removals, and on systems with a failing drive. Frequently paired with an automatic repair loop.
causes: Interrupted or failed Windows Update leaving a half-installed system file
Third-party antivirus removed or corrupted a system file
Corrupt user profile or system registry
Aggressive third-party privacy or tuning tool
fix_steps: Boot into Safe Mode and uninstall any antivirus or recently installed system tool
Hold Shift while clicking Restart, then use Troubleshoot > Advanced > Startup Repair > Restart
From an elevated Command Prompt run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth, then sfc /scannow
Uninstall the most recent Windows Update from Settings > Windows > Update history > Uninstall updates
Check drive health with chkdsk C: /scan and SMART data before reinstalling Windows
As a last resort use Reset this PC > Keep my files, which rebuilds the system while keeping your data
when_to_call_pro: Get professional help if Startup Repair loops without progress, if the drive reports failures, or if a clean Reset this PC still lands on this screen.

name: UNMOUNTABLE_BOOT_VOLUME
meaning: Windows cannot mount the drive it boots from because the filesystem is damaged. A classic result of a power cut or forced shutdown during a write.
causes: Dirty shutdown during a large write operation
Failing drive with bad sectors in the boot area
Loose or faulty SATA or NVMe connection
Sudden power loss with no battery backup or UPS
fix_steps: Boot into the Recovery Environment by interrupting booting three times, or use Shift+Restart
Open Command Prompt and run chkdsk C: /f /r /x, confirming with Y when prompted
If the drive letter is wrong, use diskpart to list volumes and substitute the correct letter
Run bootrec /fixmbr and bootrec /fixboot if the boot sector was also damaged
Check SMART health and replace the drive if it reports reallocated or pending sectors
Once repaired, back up your data immediately and consider replacing the drive
when_to_call_pro: Stop and see a professional if chkdsk cannot complete, if the drive is not detected at all, or if the data on it is irreplaceable.

name: INACCESSIBLE_BOOT_DEVICE
meaning: Windows lost access to the system partition during startup. Almost always a storage driver, BIOS storage mode, or filesystem problem rather than a broken Windows install. Moving a Windows drive to a different machine, or changing AHCI to RAID after installation, triggers it reliably.
causes: Storage controller mode or settings changed in BIOS after Windows was installed
Missing, corrupt or misbehaving storage filter drivers
Filesystem corruption on the system partition
Moving the hard disk to a different computer with a different controller
Faulty motherboard, storage controller or hardware
Corrupt files in the small SYSTEM partition
fix_steps: Unplug every storage device except the one Windows is installed on, then boot again, since a stray drive holding a broken bootloader will cause this
Enter BIOS with Del or F2 and confirm the SATA mode matches the installed configuration: AHCI for almost all modern systems
Boot into Safe Mode, which usually starts even with this fault, and check the Storage controller, file system and UpperFilters values under Services > msahci and storahci
Interrupt booting three times or hold Shift while clicking Restart to reach the Recovery Environment
From Command Prompt run bootrec /fixmbr, bootrec /fixboot and bootrec /rebuildbcd
If bootrec reports access denied, run bcdboot C:\Windows /s C: /f UEFI, using /f BIOS on a legacy machine
Run chkdsk C: /f /r /x to repair the filesystem
when_to_call_pro: Take it to a technician if Safe Mode will not start either, if the drive is missing in BIOS, or if the boot files cannot be rebuilt.

name: NTFS_FILE_SYSTEM
meaning: The NTFS driver itself crashed. The filesystem on the volume is likely damaged, or the drive is failing and returning bad data to the driver.
causes: Filesystem corruption from a forced shutdown or power loss
Bad memory or unstable RAM timings
Filter drivers from antivirus or disk encryption tools
fix_steps: Run chkdsk C: /scan first to see the damage without changing anything
Then run chkdsk C: /f /r /x to repair and scan for bad sectors
Run SMART or vendor disk tools and replace any drive reporting failures
Test RAM with MemTest86, since bad RAM corrupts files
Update chipset drivers and reinstall disk encryption or antivirus software
Back up your files as soon as the system is usable, because this stop code frequently precedes data loss
when_to_call_pro: Get help immediately if the drive is failing, because continuing to use it can destroy the remaining data on it.

name: THREAD_STUCK_IN_DEVICE_DRIVER
meaning: A driver stopped responding for too long, so Windows decided it had hung. It often appears as a freeze followed by an automatic restart with this stop code.
causes: Graphics driver stuck, often a GeForce Experience or AMD Adrenalin bug
Faulty storage, sound card or network driver
Overheating GPU causing the driver to stall
Failing drive hanging on a bad sector
Insufficient system memory with heavy paging
fix_steps: Clean reinstall GPU drivers with DDU, and disable driver auto-updates so the version does not silently change again
Update chipset, network and storage drivers
Monitor GPU temperature during the activity that triggers the freeze
Run chkdsk /scan and check disk SMART data
Disable hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling and overlay software
Verify the system drive has plenty of free space
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the freeze survives a clean driver install with stock settings and healthy temperatures.

name: CRITICAL_OBJECT_TERMINATION
meaning: A process essential to Windows was killed or terminated unexpectedly. Frequently follows a hibernation or Fast Startup failure.
causes: Hibernation or Fast Startup saving an inconsistent system state
Recently installed software or driver that conflicts with the kernel
Filesystem corruption on the system volume
fix_steps: Turn off hibernation and Fast Startup by running powercfg /h off as administrator, then verify Fast Startup is off in Power Options
Run chkdsk C: /scan and then chkdsk C: /f /r /x
Test RAM with MemTest86
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow
Uninstall the last few software updates and drivers and retest
when_to_call_pro: Escalate if disabling Fast Startup does not help and both memory and disk tests pass, since that narrows the fault to firmware or board-level issues.

name: TRAP_CAUSE_UNKNOWN
meaning: A fault occurred that Windows could not attribute, and the specific cause depends on the system that produced it. Commonly seen as a generic crash after a failed update.
causes: Aggressive disk cleanup tool deleted system files
fix_steps: Run sfc /scannow from an elevated Command Prompt
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth, which is often required before sfc can repair anything
Reboot and repeat sfc /scannow, since DISM often needs two passes
Uninstall the most recent Windows Update if the problem started right after one
Check disk health, because a failing drive cannot hold a repaired file
when_to_call_pro: Ask for help if sfc cannot repair the file even after DISM and a reboot, or if the drive is failing.

name: DRIVER_POWER_STATE_FAILURE
meaning: A driver failed to complete a power management request within the time Windows allows. Very common on laptops with ageing batteries and on systems with aggressive power management drivers.
causes: Aggressive or faulty power management and chipset drivers
Failing battery or charger on a laptop
Graphics driver stalling during sleep transitions
USB device preventing sleep, such as a phone charger or webcam
Dying CMOS battery giving unreliable firmware power states
Fast Startup saving an inconsistent state
fix_steps: Update chipset, graphics and power management drivers from your PC vendor
Run powercfg /h off to disable hibernation, then retest sleep and wake
Unplug all USB devices and try sleep again to rule out a device blocking the transition
On a laptop, run the manufacturer's battery health report to check charge capacity
Replace the CMOS battery if the clock resets every time the PC is off
Set the power plan's sleep timeout to Never while testing
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the machine cannot complete a sleep cycle at all, or if the battery report shows heavy degradation.

name: KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE
meaning: A kernel-level safety check caught a driver trying to access memory it should not. Usually a driver bug or an intrusion-detection driver hooking the kernel.
causes: Intrusion prevention or antivirus filter driver conflict
Out-of-date or mismatched driver, often graphics or storage
Incompatible third-party tool such as an RGB or monitoring utility
fix_steps: Boot Safe Mode and uninstall third-party antivirus, VPN, RGB and system monitoring tools
Update chipset and GPU drivers to current versions
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow to verify system file integrity
Test RAM with MemTest86
Reinstall the security software cleanly rather than layering it back on
when_to_call_pro: Get help if the fault persists with all third-party security and monitoring software removed and a clean driver install.

name: DPC_WATCHDOG_VIOLATION
meaning: A driver spent far too long in a Deferred Procedure Call, which Windows uses for urgent low-level work. The named driver is almost always the cause, with network and storage drivers leading the list.
causes: Faulty network adapter driver, very often Realtek or Wi-Fi
Failing storage, NVMe or RAID driver
USB device or hub driver stalling
Incompatible virtualisation or VPN filter driver
fix_steps: Update the named driver from its vendor, starting with network and storage
Clean reinstall the GPU driver with DDU if that is the one named
Test RAM with MemTest86
Disconnect external USB devices and retest
Check disk SMART data and run chkdsk /scan
Remove VPN clients and virtualisation tools and retest
when_to_call_pro: Take it in if the named driver is a Microsoft storage driver and both disk health and memory tests pass, because that points at the controller or board.

name: BAD_POOL_CALLER
meaning: A driver passed a bad parameter to a kernel function, usually from a corrupted driver or a badly written hook into Windows internals.
causes: Antivirus or monitoring tool hooking system calls incorrectly
Corrupted system file after an update
fix_steps: Identify the driver named in brackets and update or reinstall it
Remove third-party antivirus, tuning and monitoring software and retest
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth then sfc /scannow
Test RAM with MemTest86
Update chipset drivers
when_to_call_pro: Ask a technician if the named driver cannot be identified or is a core Microsoft file.

name: DRIVER_CORRUPTED_EXPOOL
meaning: Windows found corruption in memory a driver had allocated from the general kernel pool. Almost always points to a specific faulty driver, with graphics, network and storage drivers most common.
causes: Corrupted graphics, network or storage driver
fix_steps: Note the driver name and reinstall it cleanly from the official vendor
Update chipset drivers first, since they underpin everything else
Test RAM with MemTest86
Check disk health and run chkdsk /scan
Run sfc /scannow and DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
when_to_call_pro: Seek help if the fault survives a clean driver install and clean memory and disk tests.

name: KERNEL_DATA_INPAGE_ERROR
meaning: Windows could not read a page of memory from disk while paging. The drive could not deliver the data, so the underlying problem is almost always storage rather than software.
causes: Failing or dying hard drive or SSD
Loose or damaged SATA, NVMe or power cable
Corrupted page file or hibernation file
Excessive memory pressure from too many programs
Failing controller on the drive or motherboard
Windows crashed during a large write
fix_steps: Back up your important files immediately, because this stop code predicts drive failure
Check SMART data with the vendor's tool or PowerShell Get-PhysicalDisk
Run chkdsk C: /scan, then chkdsk C: /f /r /x
Reseat the drive's data and power cables, or reseat the M.2 screw
Confirm the system drive has generous free space
Replace the drive if SMART reports reallocated, pending or uncorrectable sectors
when_to_call_pro: Replace the drive or see a professional immediately if SMART shows failures. Continuing to use a drive in this state risks losing everything on it.

name: HAL_INITIALIZATION_FAILED
meaning: A hardware abstraction layer driver failed while the system was starting, so the screen never appears. This is a boot-time hardware or firmware problem.
causes: Incompatible or corrupted storage controller driver
Storage controller mode changed in BIOS after installation
Corrupted system files in the boot partition
fix_steps: Enter BIOS and confirm the SATA mode matches the installed Windows configuration
Boot into Windows Recovery and rebuild the boot files with bcdboot C:\Windows /s C: /f UEFI
Run chkdsk C: /f /r /x from the recovery command prompt
Check disk health and replace the drive if it reports failures
Load BIOS defaults, which clears an overclocked or misconfigured memory setting
Update chipset and storage controller drivers from your PC vendor
when_to_call_pro: Call a technician if the drive is not detected in BIOS at all, since no software fix will help at that point.

name: PROCESS1_INITIALIZATION_FAILED
meaning: Windows could not start its very first user-mode process. This happens early in boot and points at corrupted system files or a failing drive.
causes: Corrupted system files from a failed update
Aggressive startup tool or antivirus blocking boot
Insufficient disk space for the boot partition
fix_steps: Boot into Safe Mode or the Recovery Environment
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth then sfc /scannow
Run chkdsk C: /f /r /x
Uninstall the last Windows Update or recently installed startup software
Verify free space on the system drive
Check disk SMART data before considering a reinstall
when_to_call_pro: Get help if the drive reports failures or if Safe Mode will not load either.

name: DRIVER_VERIFIER_DETECTED_VIOLATION
meaning: Driver Verifier deliberately crashed the system to prove a driver is faulty. This is not a hardware fault; Verifier is a diagnostic tool that was switched on, usually by a support technician.
causes: Driver Verifier was enabled previously, sometimes by a support technician
A genuinely faulty driver that Verifier has now identified
fix_steps: Boot into Safe Mode, which Driver Verifier normally ignores
Open an elevated Command Prompt and run verifier /reset, then reboot
If you cannot reach Safe Mode, boot from Windows install media and choose Repair > Command Prompt, then run verifier /reset
Reboot normally, and the system will now start without the check
Update the drivers that were being verified, especially chipset and GPU
Re-enable Verifier in small batches only if you need to keep diagnosing a specific fault
when_to_call_pro: Get help if you cannot boot into Safe Mode or the Recovery Environment, since verifier /reset must be run from one of those.

name: VIDEO_TDR_FAILURE
meaning: The graphics driver stopped responding and Windows tried to reset it, then gave up. This is the graphics driver hung family of errors, often accompanied by a black screen and sound cutting out.
causes: Graphics driver bug, frequently after a driver update
GPU overheating or a failing GPU
Unstable overclock or undervolt on the GPU
Failing power supply unable to hold up under graphics load
Loose or reseated GPU or its power cables
fix_steps: Clean reinstall the GPU driver with DDU in Safe Mode, then install the newest stable driver
Disable driver auto-updates in Windows Update so your version is not replaced unexpectedly
Reset every GPU overclock and undervolt, including profiles in the vendor's own app
Monitor GPU temperature while reproducing the fault, and clean dust from the cooler
Test RAM with MemTest86, since video workloads stress memory hard
Check the GPU power cables are fully seated and the PSU has adequate capacity
when_to_call_pro: Take it to a technician if the fault persists at stock clocks with clean memory tests, because that points at the GPU, the PSU or the motherboard.

name: VIDEO_TDR_TIMEOUT_DETECTED
meaning: A display or miniport driver did not respond in time and Windows could not recover the GPU. Frequently follows a graphics driver update or a multi-monitor configuration change.
causes: Graphics driver fault after an update
Dangling or unsupported monitor configuration, HDMI or DisplayPort quirks
Third-party overlay or capture software hooking the display driver
fix_steps: Roll back or clean reinstall the graphics driver with DDU
Reconnect display cables and test with a single monitor to isolate multi-monitor issues
Remove overlays, wallpapers and hardware-accelerated apps
Check GPU temperatures and clear dust from the cooler
Update chipset drivers and the monitor's driver through Windows Update
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the fault survives a clean driver install on a single monitor at stock clocks.

name: VIDEO_SCHEDULER_INTERNAL_ERROR
meaning: The graphics scheduler found an internal inconsistency, usually right after waking from sleep or after a display change.
causes: Graphics driver bug on a sleep or wake transition
Failing GPU or unstable GPU memory
fix_steps: Update the GPU driver cleanly with DDU
Set the GPU's power management mode to Balanced or Optimal rather than Maximum Performance
Reset overclocks and undervolts
Update chipset drivers
Test RAM and check GPU temperature under load
when_to_call_pro: Get help if the fault only appears on wake and survives a clean driver install, since it can indicate a failing GPU.

name: DRIVER_RETURNED_HOLDING_CANCEL_LOCK
meaning: A driver failed to release a lock it held after an operation was cancelled, which leaves the kernel unable to continue safely.
causes: Failing drive hanging on a bad sector
fix_steps: Update storage and network drivers from their vendors
Check disk SMART data and run chkdsk /scan
Test RAM with MemTest86
Clean reinstall the driver in Safe Mode
when_to_call_pro: Take it in if disk health and memory are clean, since the fault then points at the storage controller or board.

name: POOL_CORRUPTION_IN_FILE_AREA
meaning: Windows found corruption in a memory allocation used for files. Usually a driver wrote past the end of a buffer, frequently storage or networking related.
causes: Buggy storage or network filter driver
Antivirus or disk encryption filter driver
fix_steps: Update storage controller and chipset drivers from your PC vendor
Update your SSD or NVMe firmware to the latest release
Temporarily uninstall antivirus and disk encryption software to test
Test RAM with MemTest86
Check disk SMART data and run chkdsk /scan
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the fault repeats across storage driver versions with healthy SMART data, since the drive itself may be failing.

name: WHEA_UNCORRECTABLE_ERROR
meaning: The Windows Hardware Error Architecture found a hardware fault it could not correct, usually a CPU, memory or PCIe error reported by the processor itself. This is one of the clearest hardware-failure indicators on Windows.
causes: Failing CPU, often a dying core or unstable overclock
Defective RAM or an unstable memory overclock
Failing motherboard or power supply delivering unstable voltage
Exotic hardware such as an old server board or a modified system
Failing PCIe device such as a GPU or NVMe drive
fix_steps: Note the four parameters at the bottom of the screen, since they identify whether the fault is in the processor, memory or a specific PCIe slot
Load BIOS defaults and remove every overclock and undervolt, including memory timings
Test RAM with MemTest86 and try one stick at a time in each slot
Check CPU and VRM temperatures under load and improve case airflow
Remove all expansion cards one at a time to isolate a failing PCIe device
Update BIOS and chipset drivers to current versions
Check the PSU under load with a tester, since unstable voltage produces this fault
when_to_call_pro: This code is a hardware-level warning and usually needs a technician. Go if the fault persists at stock settings with clean memory tests and no overheating, because that points at the CPU, board or PSU.

name: FAULTY_HARDWARE_CORRUPTED_PAGE
meaning: Windows detected that the hardware itself returned corrupted memory. This is a strong signal of failing RAM, a failing CPU or an unstable power supply feeding the memory.
causes: Failing CPU or motherboard memory controller
Failing power supply delivering unstable voltage to memory
fix_steps: Run MemTest86 for several full passes and record every failing address
Test one stick at a time in each slot to isolate a module or slot fault
Disable XMP/EXPO and any memory overclock
Improve case airflow and check CPU and memory temperatures under load
Test the PSU with a load tester or swap in a known-good unit
Reseat the CPU and check cooler mounting pressure if the fault persists across all RAM
when_to_call_pro: This code is a hardware-level warning. See a technician if a single failing address repeats, since that identifies a specific module.

name: CRITICAL_STRUCTURE_CORRUPTION
meaning: Windows detected corruption in a critical internal structure it relies on. This is serious and usually indicates a driver or memory fault rather than a minor glitch.
fix_steps: Update all drivers, chipset first
Test RAM with MemTest86 over multiple passes
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow
Check disk SMART data
Remove third-party antivirus and monitoring tools to test
when_to_call_pro: Seek professional help if the fault continues after clean memory, disk and driver checks.

name: CLOCK_WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT
meaning: One of the processor's internal watchdog timers expired, usually because the processor was held in an unrecoverable state for too long. On overclocked systems it is very often an unstable CPU or memory overclock.
causes: Failing CPU or motherboard voltage regulation
Faulty PSU delivering unstable power under load
Legacy processor running out of address space, on very old hardware
fix_steps: Load BIOS defaults and remove every overclock and undervolt
Increase CPU voltage slightly in small steps only if you intend to tune, and test each change
Test RAM with MemTest86 with XMP disabled
Check CPU temperature and cooler mounting under sustained load
Update BIOS to the latest version
Test with a known-good PSU if the fault appears under heavy load
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the fault persists at stock settings with clean memory tests and good cooling, since that indicates failing CPU or board hardware.

name: DPC_WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT
meaning: A Deferred Procedure Call also ran past its deadline. This is the sibling of DPC_WATCHDOG_VIOLATION and points at a driver holding the processor too long, usually a network, storage or graphics driver.
causes: USB device or hub driver stalling
fix_steps: Update chipset, network, storage and graphics drivers
Disconnect external USB devices and retest
Test RAM with MemTest86
Check disk SMART data and run chkdsk /scan
Uninstall VPN and virtualisation software to test
when_to_call_pro: Take it in if the fault survives driver updates with clean memory and disk, since the board or a device may be generating bad interrupts.

name: DRIVER_OVERRAN_STACK_BUFFER
meaning: A driver wrote past the end of its stack allocation. Windows caught the overflow and stopped the system rather than letting it corrupt other memory.
causes: Faulty or mismatched graphics, network or audio driver
fix_steps: Identify the driver named in the message and reinstall it from the official source
Clean reinstall GPU drivers with DDU if graphics related
Uninstall third-party antivirus, tuning and monitoring tools
Test RAM with MemTest86
Run sfc /scannow
when_to_call_pro: Ask a technician if the fault persists across all driver versions and hardware tests are clean.

name: PAGE_FAULT_IN_FREED_SPECIAL_POOL
meaning: A driver used memory after it had been freed. Windows allocates special pool memory with guard pages specifically to catch this class of bug, so this code reliably identifies faulty driver code.
causes: Buggy driver using memory after freeing it
Antivirus or monitoring driver with a use-after-free bug
fix_steps: Update or reinstall the driver named in the message
Remove third-party antivirus, VPN and tuning software and retest
Clean reinstall GPU drivers with DDU if graphics related
Test RAM with MemTest86
Run sfc /scannow to verify system file integrity
when_to_call_pro: Seek help if the fault survives all driver updates and has no identifiable third-party component.

name: DRIVER_PAGE_FAULT_BEYOND_END_OF_ALLOCATION
meaning: A driver tried to use memory past the end of a buffer it had allocated. Like the freed-special-pool code, this reliably pinpoints faulty driver code rather than hardware.
causes: Driver writing past the end of an allocated buffer
fix_steps: Update or reinstall the driver named in the message
Clean reinstall GPU and chipset drivers if storage or graphics related
Remove third-party antivirus and disk filter software to test
Test RAM with MemTest86
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the fault survives driver updates and clean hardware tests.

name: ATTEMPTED_WRITE_TO_READONLY_MEMORY
meaning: A driver attempted to write to memory the operating system has marked read-only. Usually a driver bug or software built for an older Windows version.
causes: Old or mismatched driver, frequently from a device no longer supported
Antivirus, VPN or disk encryption filter driver
Partially removed software leaving a filter driver loaded
Failing RAM producing a bad pointer
fix_steps: Note the driver or module named in the stop message and identify which program owns it
Use Safe Mode to uninstall that software completely, then reboot and reinstall an up-to-date version
Update all drivers: chipset first, then GPU, then peripherals
Run the hardware changes troubleshooter and scan for hidden devices with no driver
Test RAM if the named file is a Microsoft system file rather than a third-party driver
Check Reliability Monitor for the application that was active when the crash occurred
when_to_call_pro: Contact a technician if you cannot identify the named driver, because guessing at software removal can cost you data.

name: FLTMGR_FILE_SYSTEM
meaning: The Windows file system filter manager crashed. Antimalware, backup tools, disk encryption and virtual drive software all install filter drivers here, so third-party software is the usual cause.
causes: Antivirus or backup software filter driver
Disk encryption or virtual drive filter driver
Conflicting filter drivers from two security products
fix_steps: Uninstall third-party antivirus, backup and disk encryption software one at a time and retest
Avoid running two security suites at once, since their filter drivers conflict
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow
Check disk SMART data and run chkdsk /scan
Reinstall the security software cleanly rather than restoring an old image
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the fault persists with all filter-driver software removed, since that points at the drive or system files.

name: VIDEO_DXGKRNL_FATAL_ERROR
meaning: The DirectX graphics kernel hit a fatal error inside a driver. Almost always a graphics driver problem, and a strong indicator of a driver bug rather than hardware.
causes: Graphics driver bug, often after an update
Third-party overlay or antivirus hooking the graphics stack
Insufficient system memory for the graphics workload
fix_steps: Clean reinstall GPU drivers with DDU in Safe Mode
Reset all GPU overclock and undervolt settings, including vendor app profiles
Disable overlays, screen recording and hardware-accelerated wallpaper software
Update chipset drivers
Test RAM with MemTest86 and check GPU temperature under load
Check the PSU capacity if the fault appears only in demanding games
when_to_call_pro: Take it in if the fault persists at stock clocks with a clean driver and clean memory tests.

name: VIDEO_MEMORY_MANAGEMENT_INTERNAL
meaning: The graphics driver found an internal problem managing video memory. Frequently a failing GPU, but also seen when a card runs out of memory or memory overclock is unstable.
causes: Insufficient video memory for the application or resolution
Integrated graphics running out of shared system RAM
fix_steps: Update the GPU driver to the newest stable version
Close GPU-heavy applications and lower in-game resolution or texture quality
For integrated graphics, ensure the system has enough free RAM for shared memory
Reset GPU memory overclocks and undervolts
Test with a different output cable or port to rule out a cable fault
Check GPU temperature, since dying GPUs often fail when hot
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the fault happens at low settings and low temperature, which points to failing GPU memory.

name: BITLOCKER_FATAL_ERROR
meaning: A BitLocker encryption component failed in a way that could risk data loss, so Windows halted. Frequently follows firmware, TPM or storage changes.
causes: TPM or firmware change after enabling BitLocker
BIOS update changing Secure Boot or TPM state
fix_steps: Find your BitLocker recovery key before anything else, from your Microsoft account, your organisation, or where you saved it
Boot into the Recovery Environment and enter the recovery key when prompted
Suspend BitLocker before any BIOS, TPM or hardware change: manage-bde -protectors -disable C:
Resume protection afterwards with manage-bde -protectors -enable C:
Check disk SMART data, since storage changes are a common trigger
Restore BIOS and Secure Boot settings to what they were when encryption was enabled
when_to_call_pro: Get professional help if you do not have a recovery key, because without it the data cannot be decrypted. Also seek help if the drive is failing.

name: SECURE_BOOT_VIOLATION
meaning: Windows refused to load a driver or bootloader because it was not signed as trusted under Secure Boot. Triggered by a modified BIOS setting, an old unsigned driver, or leftover bootloaders from another OS.
causes: Secure Boot disabled or set to a custom key in BIOS
Unsigned or revoked driver, often a very old chipset or LAN driver
Leftover GRUB or another OS bootloader installed
fix_steps: Note which component was blocked, usually named on the blue screen, and remove it in Safe Mode
In BIOS, check the Secure Boot setting and load the default or factory keys if they were customised
Uninstall any second operating system bootloader such as GRUB, or restore it from that OS
Install signed drivers only, from the PC vendor rather than an old third-party pack
Check BIOS for an unsigned or modified firmware state, which is a serious security concern
when_to_call_pro: Get help if Secure Boot was not deliberately disabled and the blocked component cannot be identified. If BIOS firmware itself is reported as unsigned, treat the machine as untrustworthy.

name: FATAL_ABNORMAL_RESET_ERROR
meaning: The system recorded an abnormal reset that it could not explain, which usually means a hardware reset event such as a watchdog, overheating or a power problem.
causes: Failing power supply cutting out under load
External device forcing a reset, such as a failing USB hub
fix_steps: Check CPU and GPU temperatures under sustained load and improve airflow
Test the PSU with a load tester or swap in a known-good unit
Test RAM with MemTest86 and remove all overclocks
Disconnect every external USB device and retest
Replace the CMOS battery so the firmware state is reliable
Check for any BIOS update that fixes known reset bugs on your board
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if resets continue with stock settings, clean memory tests and a known-good PSU, since that points at the board.

name: INTERNAL_POWER_ERROR
meaning: A power management driver detected an invalid internal state, usually when entering or leaving sleep, or while resuming from hibernation.
causes: Chipset and power management driver faults
Failing battery or charger on a laptop
Graphics driver stalling during a power transition
Faulty USB device preventing a clean power transition
fix_steps: Update chipset, graphics and power management drivers from your PC vendor
Run powercfg /h off to disable hibernation and Fast Startup
Disconnect all USB devices and retry the sleep cycle
On a laptop, check battery health with the manufacturer's report tool
Set the active power plan sleep timeout to Never while testing
when_to_call_pro: Get help if the machine cannot complete a power transition at all, or if the battery report shows severe capacity loss.

name: ACPI_BIOS_ERROR
meaning: An ACPI function called by Windows failed, which points at a mismatch between firmware and drivers. Very common on laptops after a BIOS update.
causes: Chipset or power management driver mismatch
ACPI setting changed in BIOS such as C-states or Wake on LAN
fix_steps: Update BIOS firmware from your PC vendor, then update chipset and power management drivers
Restore ACPI defaults in BIOS by setting C-States, Wake on LAN and PCI-E to their default values
Run powercfg /h off to disable hibernation and Fast Startup
On a laptop, verify the charger is original and the battery health report is reasonable
Run powercfg /batteryreport /output battery.html to review battery design capacity versus full charge capacity
when_to_call_pro: Get help if the fault appears immediately after a BIOS update, since the firmware may need to be rolled back or further patched.

name: HARDWARE_INTERRUPT_STORM
meaning: A device generated interrupts far faster than expected, overwhelming the system. Usually a failing device, a bad driver, or an IRQ conflict on older hardware.
causes: Failing USB device, hub or controller
fix_steps: Disconnect every external USB device and retest
Remove expansion cards one at a time to isolate the device
Update chipset, USB and network drivers from your PC vendor
Check for conflicting IRQ assignments in Device Manager > View > Resources by input/output
Reseat internal connectors such as front-panel USB headers
Test RAM with MemTest86
when_to_call_pro: Take it to a technician if the fault follows a specific internal device you cannot replace, since that usually means failing hardware.

name: REGISTRY_ERROR
meaning: The registry hive could not be read from disk, usually because the registry file itself is corrupt or the drive is failing. Data recovery matters here, not just a repair.
causes: Corrupt registry hive after a sudden power loss
Aggressive shutdown while the registry was being written
Failed update leaving the registry inconsistent
fix_steps: Boot into Safe Mode, which uses a reduced registry set and often starts
Back up your data immediately, because the registry can be rebuilt but files on a failing drive can be lost
Run chkdsk C: /scan and check disk SMART data
Restore from a System Restore point in Safe Mode using rstrui.exe
If nothing else works, use Reset this PC keeping your files, which rebuilds the registry from scratch
On an advanced system, boot into the Recovery Environment and copy hives from \Windows\System32\config\RegBack
when_to_call_pro: Get professional help immediately if the drive reports failures, because the data may not be recoverable if the drive continues to degrade.

name: SPECIAL_POOL_DETECTED_MEMORY_CORRUPTION
meaning: Windows found that a driver had corrupted memory it had allocated. Special pool memory is instrumented specifically to catch driver bugs, so this reliably points at faulty driver code.
causes: Driver overwriting memory outside its allocation
fix_steps: Update or reinstall the driver named in the message
Clean reinstall GPU drivers with DDU if graphics related
Remove third-party antivirus, VPN and tuning software and retest
Test RAM with MemTest86
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow
when_to_call_pro: Ask a technician if the fault persists across all driver versions with clean memory tests.

name: TIMER_OR_DPC_INVALID
meaning: A driver left an invalid timer or Deferred Procedure Call registered. Almost always a driver bug rather than a Windows fault.
causes: Faulty network, storage or graphics driver
Faulty hardware producing interrupts at high rates
fix_steps: Update chipset, network, storage and graphics drivers
Uninstall third-party antivirus and VPN software to test
Test RAM with MemTest86
Check disk SMART data
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow
when_to_call_pro: Take it in if the fault survives driver updates with clean memory and disk, since the board or a device may be generating bad interrupts.

name: REFERENCE_BY_POINTER
meaning: A low-level system reference pointed at an invalid memory address. Effectively the same family of fault as IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL and usually shares its causes.
fix_steps: Test RAM with MemTest86 for two full passes
Update chipset, GPU and network drivers
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth then sfc /scannow
Check disk health and free space on the system drive
Load BIOS defaults and remove overclocks, then retest
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if RAM and disk tests are clean but crashes continue across several different stop codes.

name: BAD_POOL_HEADER
meaning: The management information at the start of a kernel memory block was corrupted. This is one of the classic driver-memory-corruption codes and is very often bad RAM rather than a driver.
causes: Unstable memory overclock such as XMP or EXPO
fix_steps: Run MemTest86 for at least four full passes with XMP/EXPO disabled
Reseat and clean RAM slots, testing one module at a time
Update chipset, GPU and network drivers
Check disk SMART data and run chkdsk /scan
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow
when_to_call_pro: Take it in if a failing address repeats in MemTest86, since that identifies a specific faulty module.

name: PFN_LIST_CORRUPT
meaning: The list Windows keeps of physical memory pages is corrupt. This strongly indicates a memory fault, and it is one of the codes most reliably caused by failing RAM.
causes: Failing drive corrupting the page file
Corrupt driver writing outside its allocation
fix_steps: Run MemTest86 for four or more full passes, one stick at a time if possible
Disable XMP/EXPO and all overclocks
Check disk SMART data, since a failing drive can corrupt the page file
Update chipset and graphics drivers
Check case airflow and temperatures under load
Run sfc /scannow and DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if errors persist across every RAM module and slot with stock timings, because that points at the board or CPU.

name: FILE_SYSTEM
meaning: The core file system driver crashed with a generic file system error. Usually the volume is damaged, or a disk filter driver is at fault.
causes: Disk filter driver from antivirus or encryption software
Dirty shutdown during heavy write activity
fix_steps: Run chkdsk on each volume, using /f /r /x for the system drive
Check disk SMART data and replace any drive reporting failures
Uninstall third-party antivirus and disk encryption software to test
Update storage controller and chipset drivers
Test RAM with MemTest86, since bad RAM corrupts files
Back up your files as soon as the system is usable
when_to_call_pro: Get help if the fault recurs after chkdsk repair, since recurring filesystem errors usually mean a dying drive.

name: FAT_FILE_SYSTEM
meaning: The FAT or exFAT driver crashed. Usually seen on removable media, but it can also occur on a system partition that uses FAT.
causes: Corrupt or failing USB drive, SD card or external disk
Forced removal of removable media while writing
Corrupt FAT or exFAT partition table
fix_steps: Back up anything readable from the affected drive immediately
Run chkdsk on the drive letter, for example chkdsk F: /f
Check the drive's health with the vendor's tool and replace it if it fails
Always safely eject removable media using the system tray icon rather than yanking it
Test RAM if the same fault occurs on the internal drive
when_to_call_pro: Get help if the fault is on your internal drive rather than removable media, since that implies a hardware problem worth checking.

name: EXFAT_FILE_SYSTEM
meaning: The exFAT driver crashed. exFAT is used on large SD cards, USB drives and some camera media, so this usually points at removable storage.
causes: Failing SD card or USB drive
fix_steps: Back up readable data from the card or drive immediately
Run chkdsk X: /f using the correct drive letter
Test the card in another device to establish whether the card or the reader is at fault
Reformat the card as exFAT only after backing up, and only if it is healthy
Replace the card reader if the fault follows the machine rather than the card
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the card works fine in another device but the machine still fails, as the reader hardware is likely damaged.

name: MACHINE_CHECK_EXCEPTION
meaning: The CPU detected an unrecoverable hardware error, such as a problem reaching a device on the bus, a cache error, or an unstable voltage. This is a hardware-level fault reported by the processor itself.
causes: Unstable CPU or memory overclock, or insufficient voltage
Failing power supply delivering unstable voltage
Failing PCIe device such as a GPU or NVMe drive
fix_steps: Load BIOS defaults and remove every overclock and undervolt
Test RAM with MemTest86 at stock timings
Check CPU and VRM temperatures under sustained load and improve airflow
Remove expansion cards one at a time to isolate a failing PCIe device
Test the PSU with a load tester or swap in a known-good unit
Update BIOS and chipset drivers, and confirm any known issues for your board
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the fault continues at stock settings with clean memory tests and a known-good PSU, since this points at the CPU, board or a connected device.

name: KERNEL_STACK_INPAGE_ERROR
meaning: Windows could not read a thread's kernel stack from the page file. The drive could not supply the data, so this is a storage problem.
fix_steps: Back up your files immediately and check disk SMART data
Verify the page file is system-managed and the system drive has free space
Run chkdsk C: /f /r /x
Reseat data and power connections on the drive
Test RAM with MemTest86
Replace the drive if SMART reports any failures
when_to_call_pro: Replace the drive or see a technician if SMART shows failures, because this code usually means the drive is close to failure.

name: NO_SUCH_PARTITION
meaning: Windows could not find the partition it was configured to boot from. The partition table is damaged, was altered, or the drive letter changed.
causes: Accidental disk formatting or partitioning change
Drive moved to another machine or controller
Failed update or installer that rewrote the boot partition
fix_steps: Boot from Windows install media and choose Repair > Command Prompt
Run diskpart, then list volume, to see what Windows can see
Check the boot partition is active and has a letter assigned
Rebuild the boot files with bcdboot C:\Windows /s C: /f UEFI
Check disk SMART data; a failing drive will not hold a rebuilt table
Restore the partition table from backup if you have one
when_to_call_pro: Take it to a technician if the drive is not listed in diskpart or BIOS, since no software fix applies at that point.

name: NO_BOOT_DEVICE
meaning: Windows could not find the device it boots from. Either the storage controller is not providing a drive, or no drive is marked as bootable.
causes: Storage controller mode changed in BIOS
No bootable drive found or boot order wrong
Drive not detected due to a cabling or controller fault
fix_steps: Enter BIOS and confirm the drive is listed and set as the first boot device
Confirm the SATA mode matches the installed Windows configuration
Boot into the Recovery Environment and run bootrec /fixmbr, bootrec /fixboot and bootrec /rebuildbcd
Check drive cabling and reseat connectors, including the M.2 screw
Test the drive in another machine or with a USB enclosure
when_to_call_pro: Call a technician if the drive is missing from BIOS entirely, because that is a hardware-level problem.

name: BAD_SYSTEM_CONFIG_INFO
meaning: The hardware configuration cache Windows keeps at boot is corrupt. Often follows a BIOS change such as a memory or CPU upgrade.
causes: Hardware change not reflected in the configuration cache
BIOS update that changed hardware detection
fix_steps: Boot into the Recovery Environment and run bootrec /rebuildbcd
Rebuild the hardware configuration cache with bcdedit /set {default} bootmenupolicy legacy, then retry
Load BIOS defaults and confirm the hardware is detected correctly
Replace the CMOS battery so configuration data is reliable
Run chkdsk C: /f /r /x
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the fault appears after a hardware upgrade and persists with a rebuilt BCD store.

name: MBR_CHECKSUM_MISMATCH
meaning: Windows found that the master boot record does not match its stored checksum. The boot sector is damaged or has been altered.
causes: Boot sector virus from an older system
Failing drive returning bad sectors in the first kilobyte
fix_steps: Boot into the Recovery Environment and run bootrec /fixmbr
Then run bootrec /fixboot and bootrec /rebuildbcd
Run chkdsk C: /f /r /x to check the rest of the filesystem
Check disk SMART data
Uninstall any non-Windows bootloader such as GRUB that may have rewritten the MBR
when_to_call_pro: Take it in if bootrec /fixmbr cannot repair the record or the drive reports failing sectors.

name: WIN32K_POWER_WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT
meaning: The desktop window manager did not respond to a power transition in time, so Windows forced a restart. Extremely common on laptops after sleep or when closing the lid.
causes: Graphics driver stalling on sleep or wake
External monitor or docking station handshake issue
fix_steps: Update chipset and graphics drivers from your PC vendor
Run powercfg /h off to disable hibernation and Fast Startup
Test sleep with all external devices, including monitors and docks, disconnected
Check the lid close action in Power Options, and set it to Sleep or Hibernate deliberately
Reset GPU overclocks and check the laptop battery health report
Update BIOS firmware
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the fault happens on every sleep cycle with a clean driver install and no external devices connected.

name: BUGCODE_WIFIADAPTER_DRIVER
meaning: The Wi-Fi adapter driver detected a fatal internal fault and reported it directly. Almost always resolved by a clean driver reinstall.
causes: Incompatible driver version for the adapter
fix_steps: Uninstall the Wi-Fi adapter in Device Manager with 'Delete the driver software' ticked, then reboot
Install the official driver from your PC vendor, or from the network adapter manufacturer's site
Update chipset drivers as well, since the Wi-Fi driver depends on them
Check the adapter is not disabled by a physical switch or a BIOS setting
Try removing the adapter in Device Manager and rebooting so Windows reinstalls it
Test the adapter in another device to rule out failing hardware
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the adapter crashes even with a fresh official driver and it also fails in another computer, since the hardware is then suspect.

name: BUGCODE_USB3_DRIVER
meaning: The USB 3 driver hit a fatal fault. Usually caused by a failing USB device, hub or port rather than Windows itself.
causes: Failing USB device, hub or dock
USB 3 port or controller hardware fault
Front-panel USB header wiring or header damage
USB-C port with debris or bent pins
fix_steps: Disconnect every USB device and retest, then add them back one at a time
Try a different port, preferring a rear motherboard port over a front-panel or hub port
Update chipset and USB controller drivers from your PC vendor
Inspect and clean USB-C ports with a wooden toothpick or compressed air
Run the hardware changes troubleshooter and scan for hardware changes in Device Manager
On a desktop, reseat the front-panel USB headers
when_to_call_pro: Take it in if the fault follows a specific internal port or header, which means the connector or controller is failing.

name: BUGCODE_USB_DRIVER
meaning: The older USB driver reported a fatal fault. More common than the USB 3 code and usually points at a specific failing USB device.
causes: Failing USB device such as a keyboard, mouse or printer
USB hub overload from too many bus-powered devices
fix_steps: Disconnect all USB devices and reconnect them one at a time to find the offender
Avoid unpowered hubs with several bus-powered devices attached
Update chipset and USB drivers from your PC vendor
Try a different port, preferably one directly on the motherboard
Replace the USB cable, since a marginal cable is a very common cause
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the fault follows an internal USB port rather than a removable device.

name: SDHC_INTERNAL_FATAL_ERROR
meaning: The Secure Digital Host Controller driver failed fatally, which usually means a card reader or an SD card causing a hardware fault.
causes: Failing SD card or card reader
Faulty or outdated card reader driver
Card reader hardware damage from forcing a card in
fix_steps: Try the card in another device to confirm the card is healthy
Update the card reader driver from your laptop vendor
Reseat or replace the card reader if the fault follows the machine
Run sfc /scannow and DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
Avoid forcing cards in, since damaged contacts are the usual root cause
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the card is fine in another device but the machine still fails, as the reader hardware is likely damaged.

name: CHIPSET_DETECTED_ERROR
meaning: The chipset driver itself reported a fatal fault. This usually means a badly matched or corrupt chipset driver rather than a hardware problem.
causes: Chipset driver from the wrong vendor installed
Motherboard BIOS older than the chipset driver expects
fix_steps: Identify your exact motherboard model and install the chipset driver from its vendor only
In Safe Mode, uninstall the existing chipset drivers with 'Delete the driver software' ticked, then reinstall cleanly
Update BIOS firmware to the latest version
Load BIOS defaults and disable memory overclocks
Test RAM with MemTest86 with XMP disabled
Run sfc /scannow and DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
when_to_call_pro: Get professional help if the fault persists with the correct vendor chipset driver and current BIOS, since that points at the motherboard.

name: VIDEO_DRIVER_INIT_FAILURE
meaning: The graphics driver failed during initialisation, usually at boot. Frequently caused by a corrupt driver install or insufficient video memory.
causes: Inadequate PSU power for the card
fix_steps: Boot into Safe Mode, which uses the basic display driver
Clean reinstall GPU drivers with DDU in Safe Mode
In Safe Mode, set the GPU to stock clocks so no overclock applies at startup
Update chipset drivers
Check the card's power cables are fully seated and the PSU has sufficient capacity
Test the GPU in another slot or another machine to rule out failing hardware
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the fault survives a clean driver install at stock clocks, since that usually means the card is failing.

name: UNEXPECTED_STORE_EXCEPTION
meaning: A driver or the kernel hit an unexpected condition while saving state. Often follows a storage fault or an unclean shutdown.
causes: Insufficient free space on the system volume
fix_steps: Check disk SMART data immediately and back up your files
Run chkdsk C: /f /r /x
Verify the system drive has ample free space
Update storage controller drivers from your PC vendor
Test RAM with MemTest86
when_to_call_pro: Get help if SMART shows failures or chkdsk cannot complete, because the drive is likely failing.

name: WIN32K_CRITICAL_FAILURE
meaning: A critical function in the Windows graphical interface failed, normally after a problem with a display driver or an unstable memory allocation.
causes: Third-party window manager or overlay software
fix_steps: Clean reinstall GPU drivers with DDU in Safe Mode
Reset GPU and CPU overclocks
Test RAM with MemTest86
Remove overlays, window managers and custom shell software
Update chipset drivers and run sfc /scannow
when_to_call_pro: Take it in if the fault persists at stock settings with a clean driver and clean memory tests.

name: DRIVER_PNP_WATCHDOG
meaning: The Plug and Play manager caught a driver misbehaving when a device was added, removed or started.
causes: Buggy driver during device start or removal
Failing USB or other hot-plug device
fix_steps: Identify which device was being connected when the fault occurred
Update the driver for that device from its vendor
Update chipset and USB controller drivers
Disconnect all non-essential devices and retest
Scan for hardware changes in Device Manager > View > Action
Remove the device with 'Delete the driver software' ticked and reinstall it
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the fault follows an internal device you cannot easily replace, such as a card reader or a built-in camera.

name: CRITICAL_INITIALIZATION_FAILURE
meaning: A component critical to Windows could not initialise, so the system halted during boot. Usually a driver or firmware problem that appears before the login screen.
fix_steps: Boot into Safe Mode and uninstall recently added drivers or software
Load BIOS defaults
Reseat RAM and check the drive connections
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow from recovery
Update BIOS and chipset drivers
Check disk SMART data
when_to_call_pro: Get help if Safe Mode will not start either, since that narrows the fault to firmware or core boot hardware.

name: PASSIVE_INTERRUPT_ERROR
meaning: A device driver mishandled an interrupt that was supposed to be handled passively, meaning it cannot block other work. Usually a bug in a specific driver.
causes: Buggy network, storage or graphics driver
fix_steps: Update chipset, network, storage and graphics drivers
Disconnect external devices and expansion cards to isolate the source
Test RAM with MemTest86
Check disk SMART data
Run sfc /scannow
when_to_call_pro: Take it in if the fault survives driver updates with clean memory and disk, since the board may be at fault.

name: PDC_WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT
meaning: A driver failed to complete a Plug and Control Watchdog timeout in time, so Windows forced a restart. Often seen with storage and network drivers during heavy load.
causes: Storage or network driver stalling under load
Faulty drive hanging on a bad sector
fix_steps: Update storage, network and chipset drivers
Check disk SMART data and run chkdsk /scan
Clean reinstall GPU drivers with DDU
Verify the system drive has plenty of free space
Test RAM with MemTest86
Check for a BIOS update that fixes known watchdog timeouts
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the fault persists with current drivers, clean memory tests and healthy disk SMART data.

name: SYSTEM_THREAD_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED_M
meaning: The 64-bit variant of SYSTEM_THREAD_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED. The causes and fixes are identical; only the reporting format differs because memory addresses are wider on 64-bit systems.
causes: Faulty RAM or unstable XMP/EXPO timings
Corrupt graphics, network or antivirus driver
Bad system file after a partial update
fix_steps: Write down the bracketed code and search this site for it
Test RAM with MemTest86 for two full passes with XMP disabled
Clean reinstall GPU drivers with DDU in Safe Mode
Update chipset and network drivers
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow
Check disk SMART data
when_to_call_pro: Get help if the crash survives a clean driver install and a clean memory test with all overclocks removed.

name: KERNEL_MODE_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED_M
meaning: The 64-bit variant of KERNEL_MODE_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED, most often a graphics driver fault. Same causes and fixes.
causes: Corrupt system files or a failing drive
fix_steps: Clean reinstall the GPU driver with DDU in Safe Mode
Update chipset drivers
Test RAM with MemTest86
Reset all overclock and undervolt settings
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow
when_to_call_pro: Take it to a technician if the crash only happens under graphics load and survives a clean driver install at stock clocks.

name: THREAD_STUCK_IN_DEVICE_DRIVER_M
meaning: The 64-bit variant of THREAD_STUCK_IN_DEVICE_DRIVER. Identical causes and fixes; the machine freeze before the restart is the key symptom.
causes: Failing drive hanging on bad sectors
fix_steps: Clean reinstall GPU drivers with DDU and disable driver auto-updates
Update chipset, storage and network drivers
Check disk SMART data and run chkdsk /scan
Check CPU and GPU temperatures under load
Test RAM with MemTest86
when_to_call_pro: Take it to a technician if the hang persists at stock settings with a clean driver install and healthy hardware.

name: STATUS_CANNOT_LOAD_REGISTRY_FILE
meaning: Windows could not load a registry hive file during boot, usually the SYSTEM or SOFTWARE hive. Often accompanies a corrupted or failing system drive.
causes: Sudden power loss during a registry write
fix_steps: Boot into Safe Mode or the Recovery Environment
Try restoring the registry from \Windows\System32\config\RegBack by copying those hives over the ones in config, after renaming the originals
Run chkdsk C: /f /r /x and check disk SMART data
Use System Restore from Safe Mode with rstrui.exe
As a last resort, Reset this PC keeping your files
when_to_call_pro: See a technician before replacing registry hives manually, since it is easy to make a bootable system unbootable. If the drive is failing, recover data first.

name: WINLOGON_FATAL_ERROR
meaning: The Windows logon process failed fatally, so no user could be signed in. Frequently caused by a corrupt user profile or a failing system drive.
fix_steps: Boot into Safe Mode and sign in with a different account
Delete or rename the profile's NTUSER.DAT in C:\Users\<name> to force Windows to rebuild the profile
Run chkdsk C: /f /r /x and check disk SMART data
Uninstall third-party antivirus that may be blocking logon
Verify the system drive has plenty of free space
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow
when_to_call_pro: Get help if no account can sign in and Safe Mode fails too, and back up data before doing anything invasive if the drive is failing.

name: CPI_FIRMWARE_WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT
meaning: The firmware's watchdog timed out, which means the platform firmware hung and reset the system. Often linked to BIOS bugs and power management issues.
causes: Power management settings causing firmware hangs
fix_steps: Update BIOS firmware to the latest release from your board vendor
Load BIOS defaults and disable any unusual power or XMP settings
Test RAM with MemTest86 at stock timings
Remove all overclocks and undervolts
Check CPU and VRM temperatures under load
Check for known BIOS issues or a recommended minimum BIOS version for your CPU
when_to_call_pro: Take it in if a firmware watchdog timeout recurs on the latest BIOS at stock settings with clean memory tests, since that indicates motherboard or CPU hardware failure.

name: HARDWARE_WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT
meaning: A hardware watchdog device timed out. This is usually a firmware or power delivery problem, and it resets the machine without a full blue screen on some systems.
fix_steps: Test the PSU with a load tester or swap in a known-good unit
Load BIOS defaults and remove all overclocks
Check CPU and GPU temperatures under sustained load
Update BIOS firmware
Test RAM with MemTest86
Reseat the CPU cooler and confirm mounting pressure
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the resets continue with a known-good PSU, stock settings and good cooling, as this points at the motherboard.

name: ABNORMAL_RESET_DETECTED
meaning: The system detected an unexpected reset that was not requested by Windows or the user. It usually points at the power supply, firmware or an overheating component.
fix_steps: Test the PSU with a load tester or swap in a known-good unit
Check all power and data cables are fully seated
Load BIOS defaults and remove all overclocks
Check CPU and GPU temperatures under load and improve airflow
Replace the CMOS battery
Update BIOS firmware
when_to_call_pro: Take it in if resets continue with a known-good PSU and stock settings, since that points at the board or the electricity supply.

name: DISORDERLY_SHUTDOWN
meaning: Windows was not shut down properly and recorded the fact. It appears after a power loss or forced shutdown rather than pointing at a specific component.
causes: System hung and was reset with the reset button
fix_steps: Check the PSU if power cuts are recurring, using a load tester
Review Reliability Monitor history to see what happened before each reset
Check disk SMART data, since unexpected resets can damage a drive
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow
Test RAM with MemTest86
Check temperatures under load
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if resets keep happening with a known-good PSU, clean memory tests and healthy temperatures.

name: STORAGE_MINIPORT_ERROR
meaning: The storage miniport driver, the layer between Windows and your drive, reported a fatal error. Often a driver or firmware problem rather than physical failure.
causes: Outdated or corrupt storage miniport driver
Incompatible third-party storage or RAID software
PCIe slot or controller issue with NVMe drives
fix_steps: Update storage controller drivers and chipset drivers from your PC vendor
Update your SSD or NVMe firmware
Uninstall third-party storage, RAID or disk cloning software to test
Check disk SMART data and run chkdsk /scan
Reseat an NVMe drive and try another M.2 slot if available
Test the drive in a USB enclosure to rule out the motherboard slot
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if the fault follows a specific M.2 slot rather than the drive, since that indicates the slot or controller.

name: STORAGE_DEVICE_ABNORMALITY_DETECTED
meaning: The storage device reported behaviour that Windows considered abnormal. This is an early warning that the drive is developing a fault.
causes: Power delivery problems to the drive
fix_steps: Check SMART data and treat any failure attribute as urgent
Back up your files immediately
Reseat the data and power connections
Run chkdsk /scan on each volume
Update drive firmware and chipset drivers
Replace the drive if SMART reports failures or the fault repeats
when_to_call_pro: Replace the drive or see a technician promptly. This code commonly precedes total failure, so do not put off backups.

name: MEMORY_IMAGE_CORRUPT
meaning: The in-memory copy of a system image is corrupt, which usually means the file on disk is damaged or was read incorrectly.
fix_steps: Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth, which repairs the underlying files
Then run sfc /scannow to correct anything DISM could not
Check disk SMART data, because a repaired file cannot be written to a failing drive
Uninstall the most recent Windows Update
Test RAM with MemTest86
when_to_call_pro: Get help if DISM and sfc cannot repair the image, since the drive is then the likely cause.

name: UP_DRIVER_ON_MP_SYSTEM
meaning: A single-processor network driver was loaded on a multiprocessor system. Very rare and usually caused by an ancient driver on a modern machine.
causes: Very old network driver installed on a modern system
fix_steps: Update the network driver from your PC vendor
Uninstall the legacy driver with 'Delete the driver software' ticked and reboot
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow
Check for hidden or ghost network devices in Device Manager > View > Show hidden devices
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if a legacy device cannot be removed cleanly, since old hardware may need a specific driver version.

name: UCMUCSI_FAILURE
meaning: The USB-C and power management driver failed to initialise. Usually tied to USB-C hardware, a dock, or firmware problems on a laptop.
causes: Outdated chipset or power management driver
Incompatible USB-C charger or power bank
fix_steps: Disconnect all USB-C devices, chargers and docks, then retest
Update chipset and power management drivers from your PC vendor
Update BIOS firmware
Inspect and clean the USB-C port
Try a different certified cable and charger
Run sfc /scannow and DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
when_to_call_pro: Take it to a technician if the fault follows the laptop's own USB-C port with no devices connected, since that indicates port or board damage.

name: PF_DETECTED_CORRUPTION
meaning: The Page Frame database found corruption in its records. Like the other PFN codes, this strongly suggests a memory fault.
causes: Failing drive corrupting the page file
Corrupt driver writing outside its allocation
fix_steps: Run MemTest86 for four or more full passes
Disable XMP/EXPO and remove all overclocks
Check disk SMART data
Reseat and clean RAM slots, testing one module at a time
Update chipset and graphics drivers
when_to_call_pro: See a technician if errors persist across every module and slot at stock timings, since that points at the board or CPU.

name: LOADER_ROLLBACK_DETECTED
meaning: Windows rolled back a driver or bootloader that was crashing during boot. The machine usually starts, but the update stays uninstalled.
causes: Newly installed driver or update crashing during boot
Driver incompatible with current hardware or firmware
fix_steps: Check Settings > Windows > Update history for a rolled back update and uninstall it
Update the specific driver from its vendor to a version newer than the one that rolled back
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow
Check disk SMART data, since rollback can be triggered by a failing drive
Clear the Windows Update cache and retry the update
Test RAM with MemTest86 if the rollback repeats
when_to_call_pro: Ask a technician if rollbacks keep repeating on the same machine, since that suggests a hardware or firmware conflict.

name: MICROCODE_REVISION_MISMATCH
meaning: The CPU microcode loaded by the BIOS does not match what the operating system expects. A firmware compatibility problem rather than a Windows fault.
causes: Outdated BIOS firmware for the installed CPU
CPU swapped without a BIOS update
Unsupported CPU on an older board firmware
fix_steps: Update BIOS firmware to the version that supports your exact CPU
Check the board vendor's CPU support list before flashing
Load BIOS defaults after updating
Clear the CMOS to force the firmware to re-read the CPU, using the clear-CMOS jumper or button
Reseat the CPU and check that it is fully clicked into its socket
when_to_call_pro: See a technician before flashing BIOS on an older board, since an interrupted flash can leave a board unbootable.

name: INVALID_KERNEL_HANDLE
meaning: A kernel component tried to use a handle that was invalid or had already been closed. This is normally a driver bookkeeping bug rather than a hardware fault.
causes: Buggy driver closing a handle twice
Faulty RAM producing a bad handle value
fix_steps: Update or reinstall the driver named in the message
Clean reinstall GPU and chipset drivers if relevant
Uninstall third-party antivirus, VPN and tuning software to test
Test RAM with MemTest86
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and sfc /scannow
when_to_call_pro: Ask a technician if the fault survives all driver updates and clean memory tests.
